tagline: The loop **is** the SDK — the same `/v1/messages` endpoint, called in a loop with tool results threaded back. The model decides **what**; your code decides **whether** and **when to stop**.
summary: The Claude Agent SDK is not a more powerful model or a special endpoint. It is the **plain Messages API call, placed in a loop**. The model reads your messages and tools and responds; if it wants a tool, it emits a `tool_use` **request**; **your code** runs it and threads the result back as a new message; the loop calls the model again. It ends when the model emits `end_turn`. The central truth: **the model never executes anything** — it only asks. Claude Code is this loop with permissions, rendering, and scheduling layered on top.

sections.heading: The loop is the SDK
body: A single Messages API call is a **round trip**: you send `messages[]` plus your tool definitions, the model reads them and **responds once**. The agent SDK is **that same call, placed in a loop** — same model, same `/v1/messages` endpoint, called repeatedly with the growing conversation.

The SDK adds the **loop**, not new model power. Nothing about the model changes between a one-shot API call and an agentic run; what changes is that **your program keeps calling it**, feeding each response's consequences back in as the next request.

sections.heading: Two stop reasons, one branch
body: Every model response carries a `stop_reason`, and for the agentic loop **one branch** carries the weight. `tool_use` means the model is **asking you to run something** — it has emitted a structured request and is waiting. `end_turn` means the model is **done** and control returns to your program. (The API also signals `max_tokens` and `stop_sequence`; those don't loop — they **exit** like `end_turn`, just for a different reason.)
The model **signals**; the loop **dispatches**. The framework picks no trajectory and decides no completion — it reads the flag the model set and either runs the requested tool or exits.

sections.heading: Dispatch is your code
body: When the model requests a tool, **execution lives in the harness** — or in the SDK's tool runner — never in the model. Your code **validates** the arguments, **schedules** parallel calls, runs the tool, and appends the `tool_result` back into `messages`. The model only ever sees the **result**, never your filesystem or shell.

Because dispatch is yours, this is exactly where a **gate** can sit. This is *why* Claude Code's permission system can exist at all: the seam between `tool_use` and execution is **your code's to open**. Claude Code is this loop with **approval prompts, rendering, and scheduling** layered onto that seam — but the loop underneath is the plain one.

diagram.caption: The model asks; **your code** runs. The backward arc from `append` to `model-call` is the loop — it closes once per tool call, however many turns it takes.

nodes.label: Your `messages[]` + tool defs
nodes.note: The request you build: the conversation so far plus the tool schemas you expose. This is what the model gets to read.

nodes.label: SDK calls `/v1/messages`
nodes.note: One round trip. The model reads the context and the tools and responds. It runs nothing — it only emits text and tool-use requests.

nodes.label: `stop_reason`?
nodes.note: `tool_use` → the model wants a tool. `end_turn` → it's done. This single flag is the only branch the loop checks.

nodes.label: Harness runs the tool
nodes.note: **Your** code executes here — gate, validate, or reject. The model only *requested* the tool; it never touches your shell, FS, or network.

nodes.label: Append `tool_result` to `messages`
nodes.note: The output is threaded back as a new message. The model never saw your filesystem — only this result, which now joins the conversation.

nodes.label: `end_turn` → control returns
nodes.note: The final message crosses back to your program. The loop exits — no more model calls until you start the next turn.

scenarios.title: A turn that **calls a tool**
scenarios.note: The loop closes: the result is appended and the model is called again. Fifty tool calls in a turn is still **one loop**, run fifty times.

scenarios.title: A turn that **finishes**
scenarios.note: `end_turn` is the exit. The model's final message crosses back to your program and the loop stops — no tool ran this trip.

scenarios.title: **Intercepting** a tool call
scenarios.note: Dispatch is yours, so `run-tool` is the seam: gate, approve, or reject here. This is exactly where Claude Code's permission system sits.

misconceptions.myth: Giving Claude tools means Claude runs them.
misconceptions.reality: The model emits `tool_use` **requests**; your code — or the SDK's tool runner — **executes** them and feeds results back. The model never touches your shell, filesystem, or network.
misconceptions.why: The transcript reads as if 'Claude ran `ls`' — the request and its result sit side by side, so the dispatch step in between is invisible.

misconceptions.myth: The Agent SDK is a different, more powerful endpoint than the plain API.
misconceptions.reality: It's the **same `/v1/messages`** call. The SDK is a **loop around it** — the same model, called repeatedly with the conversation growing each pass.
misconceptions.why: 'Agent' sounds like a product or a model upgrade. It's an **orchestration pattern**: the loop is the only thing the SDK adds.

misconceptions.myth: The SDK decides when the agent is done.
misconceptions.reality: The **model** signals completion via `end_turn`. The loop just **reads the flag** and either dispatches a tool or exits — it picks no trajectory.
misconceptions.why: It feels like the framework 'runs' the agent. It's a **dispatcher**; the model drives, the loop only checks one flag and acts on it.

misconceptions.myth: Tool calls execute automatically — there's no gate.
misconceptions.reality: Because dispatch is **in your code**, every call is **interceptable**: gate it behind approval, validate the arguments, or reject it outright before it runs.
misconceptions.why: The SDK tool runner's convenience hides that the **seam is yours to open** — it auto-runs by default, so the gate looks like it isn't there.
